faqs.question: Why do people wear costumes on Halloween?
faqs.answer: People wear Halloween costumes because three older habits merged: masked mumming and guising for a reward, shop-bought character play from the 1930s, and the freedom anonymity gives. A 1976 study of 1,352 trick-or-treaters showed how strongly anonymity in a group changes children's behaviour.

faqs.question: Were Halloween costumes first meant to fool ghosts?
faqs.answer: That is a folklore theory, not a recorded fact. No dated source we could trace shows people at Samhain disguising themselves from spirits; the earliest firm records of disguised visitors in Britain are a 1418 London ban on Christmas mumming and Scottish payments to guisers in 1488.

faqs.question: When did Halloween costumes start?
faqs.answer: Masked house-visiting is documented from at least 1418, but at Christmas rather than Halloween. By 1919 an American history of the holiday described Halloween party guests who 'often come masked, as ghosts or witches'.

faqs.question: When did people start buying Halloween costumes in shops?
faqs.answer: Department stores were selling ready-made children's Halloween costumes by the early 1930s. A Woodward & Lothrop advert in The Washington Daily News on 21 October 1936 sold pirates, clowns and jockeys with the line 'satisfy that great urge to be someone else'.

faqs.question: What is guising?
faqs.answer: Guising is going door to door in disguise and performing for a small reward, a custom best known from Scotland. The Dictionary of the Older Scottish Tongue records payments to 'gysaris' who danced in 1488 and 1491, long before the word was tied to Halloween.

faqs.question: What is the difference between mumming and guising?
faqs.answer: Both mean visiting houses in disguise to perform, and the Scots dictionary defines a guiser as 'a mummer, masquerader'. Mumming is the older English and Irish word, often for winter plays, while guising is the Scottish term that later attached to Halloween.

faqs.question: Why do kids behave differently in costumes?
faqs.answer: Anonymity and being in a group loosen self-restraint, a process psychologists call deindividuation. In Diener's 1976 Halloween study, 57.2% of anonymous children in groups took extra sweets, against 7.5% of children alone who had been asked their names.

faqs.question: Does wearing a costume change how you think?
faqs.answer: The evidence is weak. A 2012 study claimed a lab coat improved attention, an idea called enclothed cognition, but a preregistered 2019 replication could not reproduce the effect, so anonymity remains the better-supported mechanism.

faqs.question: Why are so many Halloween costumes scary?
faqs.answer: Ghosts, witches and skeletons match a night tied to All Saints' Day on 1 November and prayers for the dead. Scary was never the only option, though: the 1936 store range was mostly pirates, clowns and storybook characters.

faqs.question: Do costumes affect the people who see them?
faqs.answer: They can. A 2025 Milan metro study found a pregnant-looking woman was offered a seat on 67.21% of rides when someone dressed as Batman was aboard, against 37.66% without him.

faqs.question: Can I give someone a Halloween costume digitally?
faqs.answer: SubhSandesh's interactive Halloween card ends with a Boo License showing the costume you chose for the recipient, from ghost, witch, vampire, pumpkin, black cat, skeleton, mummy or bat. It takes about 5 minutes and arrives as a private link.

faqs.question: When is Halloween in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is always 31 October: a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027. All Saints' Day follows on 1 November.

# Why Do We Wear Costumes on Halloween? What the Records Show

Why do we wear costumes on Halloween? Because three older habits merged: winter mumming and guising, where masked visitors traded a performance for food or coins; a 1930s retail push that sold children ready-made characters; and the pull of anonymity, which a 1976 field study of 1,352 trick-or-treaters measured directly. The popular line that Celts dressed up to hide from spirits is a theory, not a recorded fact.

Choosing who gets to see you is not only a costume instinct. On SubhSandesh, 38.5% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it, and 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone, so even a digital greeting is usually a private, one-screen reveal. Below are the dated records, what psychologists have measured, five explanations compared, and the cases where a costume is the wrong call.

## What is a Halloween costume, as opposed to a disguise?

A Halloween costume is clothing worn on or around 31 October to play someone or something else, usually a ghost, a monster, an animal or a fictional character. A disguise hides who you are, while a costume announces what you are playing, and Halloween outfits have swung between those two jobs for six centuries.

The old words keep that memory. The [Dictionary of the Older Scottish Tongue entry for *gysar*](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/dost/gysar) defines a guiser simply as "a mummer, masquerader", and the same dictionary dates the Older Scots verb for disguising oneself to before 1522. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027, with All Saints' Day on 1 November.

## Did the Celts wear costumes to hide from spirits?

No dated record we could trace says so. The idea that people at Samhain disguised themselves so wandering spirits would mistake them for one of their own is a folklore theory, built by later writers who read village customs back into a pre-Christian past. It may be partly right, but it should be labelled as a guess.

The written trail is more worldly. Scottish royal accounts from 1488 and 1491 record payments to *gysaris* who danced, once in Lanark and once "to the king", according to the dictionary entry above. Those were paid entertainers, and nothing in either line ties them to 31 October.

The church took a dimmer view. In 1627 the Presbytery of Lanark resolved to summon "the gysartes" and examine those "clothed in womens habit", the same entry records. Scotland's own guising story belongs on a page of its own; the point here is that disguise was a whole-winter habit, from Christmas to New Year, long before it settled on one night.

Souling fits the same pattern. Ruth Edna Kelley's 1919 history describes the poor of Staffordshire and Shropshire going about "singing for soul-cakes or money" and promising prayers for the dead, yet her account of the custom mentions no masks at all.

## The history of Halloween costumes in 4 dated records

Each record below gives the date and place, what the source actually says, and what it shows about why people dress up.

### 1. 1418, London: the city bans Christmas masks

*When and where:* Christmas 1418, the City of London. *What it says:* a proclamation translated in [Henry Riley's *Memorials of London* (1868), page 669](https://archive.org/details/b2485881x) forbids anyone to walk out at night "in eny manere mommyng, pleyes, enterludes" or other disguisings with "feynyd berdis, peyntid visers", on pain of imprisonment. *What it shows:* masked house-visiting was common enough to police. The same order told householders to hang a lit lantern outside every night of the feast; our reading is that the city answered hidden faces with lit streets.

### 2. 1488 to 1627, Scotland: guisers paid, then disciplined

*When and where:* Lanark and the Scottish court. *What it says:* treasurers paid "dansaris and gysaris" in 1488 and 1491, and a presbytery summoned cross-dressed guisers in 1627. *What it shows:* disguise began as entertainment that earned a reward, and authorities read it as licence. Both motives, payment and permission, still sit underneath a modern trick-or-treat route.

### 3. 1919, United States: masks move indoors to parties

*When and where:* Ruth Edna Kelley's [*The Book of Hallowe'en* (1919)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/20644), an American history of the holiday. *What it says:* "Often they come masked, as ghosts or witches," she writes of Halloween parties, and she notes that hosts were reviving old customs, such as going "a-souling as the English used". *What it shows:* by 1919 American costume was adult party play, consciously borrowed from Britain and Ireland, not an unbroken pagan rite.

### 4. 1936, Washington, D.C.: costumes sold as a chance to be someone else

*When and where:* the Woodward & Lothrop department store, in [an advertisement in *The Washington Daily News* of 21 October 1936](https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn82016181/1936-10-21/ed-1/?sp=7). *What it says:* "Once a year at least you should satisfy that great urge to be someone else." The children's costumes, stocked in the fourth-floor toy store, included a pirate, a clown, a jockey, a wooden soldier, Red Riding Hood and Bo Peep. *What it shows:* by the mid-1930s the costume was a shop product, and the sales pitch was identity play rather than protection from the dead.

That 1936 range also carried national and ethnic caricatures that no store would stock now. The reason the custom changed is plain in the advert: retailers sold whatever character children wanted to become that year.

## What psychology says a costume does

Two field studies, fifty years apart, measure what a costume changes. One looks at the person wearing it, and the other at the people who see it.

### What a costume does to the wearer

In 1976 Ed Diener and three colleagues ran their experiment on Halloween night itself, at 27 Seattle homes. Their paper on [deindividuation among trick-or-treaters](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1976-20842-001) told 1,352 trick-or-treaters to take one sweet, then left the room, with a bowl of pennies and nickels nearby.

Anonymity and company together changed the result most. Only 7.5% of children who came alone and were asked their name and address took extra, against 57.2% of children in anonymous groups. When one child was made responsible for an anonymous group, 80.0% transgressed, 64 of 80.

A newer idea, "enclothed cognition", claims clothes change thinking through their symbolic meaning. Hajo Adam and Adam Galinsky reported in 2012 that a lab coat improved attention, but a preregistered 2019 replication by Devin Burns and colleagues could not reproduce the effect. So the best-supported mechanism is anonymity, not the outfit's magic.

### What a costume does to everyone else

In 2025 a Milan team led by Francesco Pagnini tested a costume on bystanders. In their [metro study of the "Batman effect"](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12583732), a woman who appeared pregnant boarded a train across 138 rides, sometimes with a second researcher in a Batman suit entering by another door.

Someone offered her a seat on 67.21% of observed rides when Batman was present, against 37.66% without him. Oddly, 44% of those who stood up said they had not seen Batman at all, which the authors read as an unexpected event lifting attention. A costume, in other words, also works on the audience.

## Five explanations for Halloween costumes compared

The table compares the five common explanations by their earliest dated evidence, the kind of evidence, and how firmly it holds. The rows run from weakest to strongest.

| Explanation | Earliest dated evidence | Evidence type | How firm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hiding from spirits at Samhain | No dated record found | Later folklore theory | Unproven |
| Mumming and guising for a reward | 1418 London ban; 1488 Scottish payments | Civic and royal records | Strong, but winter-wide |
| Party masks and revived customs | 1919, Kelley's history | Contemporary book | Strong for the US |
| Shop-bought character play | 1936 department-store advert | Newspaper advertisement | Strong |
| Anonymity and attention effects | 1,352 children (1976); 138 rides (2025) | Field experiments | Measured, context-bound |

The takeaway: the most repeated explanation has the thinnest evidence, and the best-documented reasons are performance, shopping and anonymity.

## Sending a costume to one person instead of a crowd

A costume is chosen for a crowd of neighbours, but a Halloween greeting is chosen for one person. Pages built on SubhSandesh average 11.1 views each, which suggests a personal page gets reopened rather than glanced at once.

For a friend, sibling or partner, the [interactive Halloween card with up to six photos](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes to make. They knock three times, carve a jack-o'-lantern and read your letter by flashlight, and it ends with a Boo License showing the costume you picked for them: ghost, witch, vampire, pumpkin, black cat, skeleton, mummy or bat.

If you want more room, the [cinematic Halloween website with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes, holds up to 12 photos, can stay locked until a time you set and has a reply box for one answer of up to 280 characters. For a non-Halloween occasion, the [full template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) lists every other page type.

## When a costume, or this page, is the wrong choice

Some costumes do harm the history above explains. The 1936 advert sold ethnic caricatures as fun, and a costume built on a real culture or a real tragedy still reads that way to the people it depicts.

- **Anonymous groups of children:** the 57.2% figure is a reason for an adult to walk with them, not a reason for alarm.
- **Grief:** a death-themed costume can land badly in a house mourning someone, so ask first.

SubhSandesh is the wrong tool for parties, costume shopping or group invitations. Both Halloween templates are one-person greeting pages with an English interface, and a recipient without a phone or laptop browser is better served by a handwritten card.

- Riley, H. T. (ed.), *Memorials of London and London Life*, Longmans (1868), p. 669.
- Kelley, R. E., *The Book of Hallowe'en* (1919), Project Gutenberg edition.
- Woodward & Lothrop advertisement, *The Washington Daily News*, 21 October 1936, p. 7, Library of Congress.

structuralLimitations: SERP: 1 WebSearch call (US index), 14 October 2026, plus 1 DuckDuckGo HTML query used only to locate the Diener 1976 paper (2 searches total). Results: mentalfloss.com (two URLs, same article), ipsnews.net (two URLs, spam syndication), insideuni.uni.edu (2020), aol.com (syndication, 404 on fetch), webbweekly.com (2020 local weekly), storyworks2.scholastic.com (paywalled, judged from snippet) and a duplicate scholastic perf-host URL. Weak count: 6 of 9 (ipsnews x2, aol syndication 404, scholastic perf duplicate, scholastic paywall, webbweekly). Overlap with sibling history-of-halloween / why-is-halloween-celebrated SERPs: 0 shared URLs measured in this run.

Brief/SERP claim checked: the SERP (Mental Floss, UNI, Webb Weekly) states Celts disguised at Samhain to hide from spirits as fact. No dated primary record of that was found; the post labels it theory. Webb Weekly's 'earliest mention ... 1585 in Scotland' could not be verified; DOST records guisers from 1488 (not tied to Halloween), so the post uses 1488 and omits 1585.

Ronald Hutton's Stations of the Sun (OUP 1996) was requested by the task prompt but is not readable: the Internet Archive copy is restricted ('item not available') and Google Books API was over quota. The post therefore does not attribute any claim to Hutton rather than cite him from memory.

Mass-produced costume claim: the SERP credits A. S. Fishbach and Ben Cooper with 1930s mass production; neither could be verified at a primary source, so the post uses a dated 1936 department-store advert (Library of Congress) instead and names no manufacturer. A 1932 Hecht Co. advert (30 boxed characters, sizes 1-14) was also read but not cited to stay within 6 outbound links. Chronicling America OCR text pages are behind a Cloudflare challenge; the advert text was read via the loc.gov JSON search API, not by working around the wall.

Enclothed cognition: Adam & Galinsky 2012 and Burns et al. 2019 are both published by Elsevier (JESP, banned publisher) and are named in prose without links; the replication claim rests on its PsyArXiv abstract.

Diener 1976: 'anonymity' in that study meant the experimenter did not ask costumed children their names; the post reports the condition rates exactly as Table 1 gives them and does not claim costumes alone caused the effect.

Concurrent sibling halloween-in-scotland owns guising detail; this post keeps Scotland to one short paragraph and two dictionary-dated records. Sibling ideas avoided: 1898 Vancouver, 1911 Kingston, Thanksgiving maskers, the Dennison Bogie Book and NRF spending figures.
